author: guido-manuel-de-la-torre-olvera
description: In 19th-century portraits, nobody smiles. Slow cameras get the blame, but the real reason lies in three centuries of portrait rules.

hero.hook: They are not unhappy, and the camera is not too slow: they are sitting for a portrait.

blocks.text: Photography started with a room, not a camera. The [[camera obscura]] is a dark chamber with a small hole: light passing through it throws an upside-down image of the outside world onto the far wall. Described in ancient China and studied from the Greeks to Leonardo da Vinci, it shows the image. It cannot keep it.

Keeping it took until **1826**, when a French inventor, [[Nicéphore Niépce]], captured the view from his window at Le Gras: the oldest surviving photograph from nature. He worked with bitumen, and the plate sat in the camera for **hours**. Niépce later partnered with another inventor, Louis Daguerre, who replaced the bitumen with a more sensitive resin. Even then, nobody sat for a portrait: nothing alive can hold still that long.

By **1837**, Daguerre had a working process: a silver-plated sheet made sensitive with iodine vapor, developed over mercury vapor and fixed in hot salt water. This was the [[daguerreotype]]. The [[exposure time]] dropped from several hours to a few minutes.

In **1838**, he pointed his camera at the Boulevard du Temple, one of the busiest streets in Paris. The photograph shows an empty city: every carriage and every pedestrian crossed the frame too fast to leave a mark on the plate.

blocks.caption: Daguerre's Boulevard du Temple, 1838: at bottom left, the man having his boots polished.

blocks.text: Except one. A man having his boots polished stayed still for the whole exposure and became the first human being ever photographed. He is in the picture because he was not moving. In **1839**, France bought the process and gave it to the world: the news was a sensation.

That same year, in **Philadelphia**, [[Robert Cornelius]] set up a camera outside his family's shop, uncovered the lens, walked into the frame and waited. The result: the oldest surviving photographic self-portrait. Hair untidy, arms folded, eyes turned to one side. He is not smiling.

This is where the usual explanation starts to fail. Lenses got faster, the chemistry improved, and within a few years a portrait needed **seconds**. By the **1850s**, a photographer could catch a sitter in the time it takes to draw a breath.

So the faces should relax. They do not. For another **fifty years**, almost everyone who sat for a camera looked straight ahead with their mouth firmly closed. The slowness of the cameras no longer explains anything: the answer lies elsewhere.

The real answer is that a photograph was not a [[snapshot]]. It was a portrait, and portraiture already came with **three hundred years** of rules inherited from painting. Painters knew what a wide smile signaled, and it was not happiness.

blocks.caption: Malle Babbe, by Frans Hals (Gemäldegalerie, Berlin), detail: a wide-open laugh, the mark of madness or drunkenness in painting.

blocks.text: The art historian [[Angus Trumble]], who wrote a history of the smile, puts it bluntly: a broad grin read as a sign of madness, drunkenness or stupidity. A saint might wear a faint one. A respectable person posing for their portrait did not.
Teeth play a part too. For Angus Trumble, it is dentistry, not shyness, that eventually let people open their mouths in front of the lens.

So the first photographers copied the painters. You sat straight, you looked at the lens, you kept your mouth shut. What the picture recorded was the sitter's dignity, not their mood: seriousness was a posture, not a state of mind.

The rule was not absolute, and the exceptions give it away. In an **1847** photograph, one of two officers from the Mexican-American War is grinning. In an **1853** picture of a card game, one player smiles while the other studies his hand. In **1860**, a man boxes, fists up, clearly enjoying himself.

None of them were having their likeness taken. They were doing something, and the camera happened to be there. What changed everything was the snapshot: cheap cameras put photography in the hands of people who were not posing, and by the **1920s** the smile had become the expected face.

events.title: The smile takes over

blocks.text: We inherited that reflex, which is why the **19th century** looks so unhappy to us. It was not. These men and women held themselves the way people did in front of a painter, upright and serious: they were striking a pose.
If nobody smiles in old photographs, it is not because cameras were slow: it is the rule of the portrait, inherited from painters, for whom a broad grin signaled madness or drunkenness.

sections.title: They smile when nobody is posing
